In mathematics, an '''ancient solution''' to a [[differential equation]] is a solution that can be extrapolated backwards to all past times, without singularities. That is, it is a solution "that is defined on a time interval of the form {{math|(−∞, ''T'')}}."<ref name="perelman">{{citation
 | last = Perelman | first = Grigori | author-link = Grigori Perelman
 | arxiv = math/0211159
 | title = The entropy formula for the Ricci flow and its geometric applications
 | year = 2002| bibcode = 2002math.....11159P}}.</ref>

The term was introduced by [[Richard S. Hamilton|Richard Hamilton]] in his work on the [[Ricci flow]].<ref>Hamilton, Richard S. The formation of singularities in the Ricci flow. Surveys in differential geometry, Vol. II (Cambridge, MA, 1993), 7–136, Int. Press, Cambridge, MA, 1995</ref> It has since been applied to other [[geometric flow]]s<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Loftin | first1 = John
 | last2 = Tsui | first2 = Mao-Pei
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Journal of Differential Geometry]]
 | mr = 2406266
 | pages = 113–162
 | title = Ancient solutions of the affine normal flow
 | volume = 78
 | year = 2008| doi = 10.4310/jdg/1197320604
 | arxiv = math/0602484
 | s2cid = 420652
 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Daskalopoulos | first1 = Panagiota | author1-link = Panagiota Daskalopoulos
 | last2 = Hamilton | first2 = Richard | author2-link = Richard S. Hamilton

 | issue = 3

 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
